The pi-pstack process that runs an automation is the only one that talks to Slack and the tracker. It performs every read of the source thread, every post, and every tracker write. Workers return findings and an optional tracker request, and have no tool for any of those writes.

`node scripts/benny-setup.mjs --project <target-repository> --check-connectors` checks the items below with read-only calls to Slack and `gh`, posts nothing, and exits nonzero when one fails. Its report names each check.

Check, in this order:

1. The Slack connector. `~/.pi/agent/pstack/credentials/slack.json` must hold `{ "token": "xoxb-..." }` with mode 0600. The bot needs `conversations.replies` read access and `chat.postMessage` in the source channel. When `slack.operations_channel_id` names a channel, which must not be the source channel, repro also needs `chat.postMessage`, `chat.update`, and `conversations.history` there for its one status message and its replies. Repro also uses `files:write` to attach the evidence a confirmed repro names to its one source reply; without it the reply links the operations thread instead. An empty value disables the operations thread and the status stays in the run log. Without the file, the automation does not start. Never put the token in YAML or in any committed file.
2. The tracker. With `tracker.type: "github"`, run `gh auth status` as the user that will run the automation and confirm `gh api repos/<owner>/<name>` succeeds. The automation treats an unreachable repository as a missing prerequisite and logs each case `blocked` instead of guessing. With any other tracker type, the skill named by `tracker.adapter_skill_name` must be one Pi can load for the project, by the locations section 3 lists, and the MCP servers it uses must be configured for the project (`pi mcp list`). The automation starts one worker per tracker write. That worker has Pi's MCP, loads the skill, searches for the action marker before any write, writes only when the marker is absent, and returns a JSON result. A missing or unresolvable skill logs the case `blocked` with the skill name, and nothing is written.
3. The webhook secret. `benny-setup.mjs` creates `~/.pi/agent/pstack/credentials/<automation name>.json`. The event sender presents its `key` as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` on `POST /events`.
4. For repro and fix, the parent pushes the worker's run branch and opens the draft pull request. That needs `gh` access to the `repository.url` repository, and the project's `origin` remote must be that repository. A worker is told to do neither, and the parent never opens a pull request that is ready for review.

## 7. Prepare the live automations

Ask whether this is first-time creation or configuration of existing automations.

Read `../../FOR_AGENTS.md` from the copied pack as the primary user-intent source for either path. Use it to understand the two triggers, tools, instructions, outcomes, and shared rules.

### First-time creation

Create one automation at a time.

For each automation:

1. Read the matching copied prompt template as secondary internal source material.
2. Turn `FOR_AGENTS.md`, the finished Benny configuration, and the template intent into a complete natural-language request.
3. Tell the live prompt to read and follow its exact committed operational file under `.cursor/automations/benny/`.
4. Use the stable repository-relative path, not a plugin source or cache path. Do not copy the operational file contents into the live prompt.
5. Read and follow the built-in `automate` skill.
6. Let `automate` discover Slack channels, the repository, and connected integrations.
7. Let `automate` confirm that the copied pack and any referenced configuration files are committed in the same repository where the automation will run.
8. Let `automate` show its draft table, obtain approval, ask readiness, and open the Automations editor.
9. Finish the editor handoff for this automation before starting the next one.

Give `automate` this complete triage intent, filled from configuration:

- Name `benny-triage`.
- Read and follow `.cursor/automations/benny/skills/triage-issue-reports/SKILL.md` for every run.
- Trigger on each new top-level report in the configured source Slack channel.
- Read the triggering thread and reply only inside it.
- Use the configured issue-tracker integration.
- Classify, inspect evidence, trace cause, dedupe, and create only clear new bugs.
- End one thread-only verdict with the configured `[benny:bug]`, `[benny:performance]`, or `[benny:other]` marker and optional tracker URL.
- Never post a source-channel root message.

After the triage editor handoff is complete, give `automate` this complete repro and fix intent:

- Name `benny-reproduce`.
- Read and follow `.cursor/automations/benny/skills/reproduce-and-fix-issues/SKILL.md` for every run.
- Trigger on the same new top-level reports in the configured source Slack channel.
- Use the configured repository and default branch.
- Read the source thread and reply only inside it.
- Include pull request creation and the configured tracker, control-adapter, and feature-map requirements. Paraphrase mapped user paths and states unless `automate` confirms an eligible committed file in the same repository.
- Wait for a trusted triage marker before acting.
- Reproduce the exact symptom twice through the mapped real UI and capture evidence.
- Verify an existing fix without authoring over it.
- Attempt an optional bounded fix only after confirmed repro, then open a draft pull request when proof and checks pass.
- Never post a source-channel root message.

Do not duplicate `automate`'s Slack, repository, integration, completeness, authentication, draft-review, approval, readiness, or editor-handoff work.

### Existing automations

The built-in `automate` skill is creation-only. Do not use it to search for, inspect, or update existing automations.

Finish configuration, routing, control-adapter, and feature-map validation. Then give the user this concise editor checklist.

For the existing triage automation, update:

- Name and description
- Direct instruction to read `.cursor/automations/benny/skills/triage-issue-reports/SKILL.md`
- New top-level Slack report trigger and source channel
- Slack thread read and reply capabilities
- Issue-tracker integration

- Repository and default branch

- Pull request action
- Tracker, control-adapter, and feature-map requirements
- Paraphrased marker wait, evidence, verification, and bounded-fix instructions

Ask the user to update each existing automation directly in its Automations editor. Do not create replacements or duplicates.

### Creation boundary

Never call a direct automation backend service or backend automation tool. Never use a browser URL that carries draft fields. Never build or open a Cursor protocol deep link. For new automations, the only finish path is the built-in `automate` skill's reviewed Automations editor handoff.

Do not enable either automation until the thread-safety test passes after the editor save.

## 7. Start the automations

Read `../../FOR_AGENTS.md` from the copied pack as the primary user-intent source. Use it to understand the two triggers, outcomes, and shared rules, and `../../templates/triage-automation-prompt.md` and `../../templates/reproduce-automation-prompt.md` for what each case's worker is told.

Start one automation at a time, and only after the user asks:

1. Read the automation names from `.pi/benny/configuration.yaml`: `automations.triage_name` and `automations.reproduce_name`.
2. Run `/pstack automation start <triage name>`. It starts the receiver as a watch worker in tmux on this machine.
3. Run `/pstack automation status <triage name>` and read the receiver URL from it. Point the user's Slack event sender at that URL (`POST /events`, bearer key from step 3 of section 4).
4. Start repro and fix the same way with `/pstack automation start <reproduce name>` once section 6 passes. Repro dispatches a case only when the tracker, the control skill, the feature map, and a trusted triage marker in the source thread all hold.

To change an automation that already exists, validate the configuration, then stop and start it. Never start a second source for a name that is already running. `start` refuses one that is.

Never write the event log, the outbox, a cursor, or a credential file by hand. Never run the serve script directly. `/pstack automation start <name>` is the only path, because it records the source as a run the operator can stop.

Do not enable normal traffic until the thread-safety test passes.

spans.replacement:
**Workers.** A subagent here is a pstack worker: an independent Pi process in tmux. To spawn one, write `brief.md` and `assignment.json` under `.pi/pstack/runs/<runId>/workers/<workerId>/` and call `pstack_worker` with `{ action: "spawn", runId, assignmentPath }`. Every assignment has `schemaVersion: 1`, `runId`, `workerId`, `kind` (`"pi"` for a Pi worker, `"watch"` for a watch), `role`, `model`, `thinkingLevel`, `workspace`, and `skills`. `skills` and `thinkingLevel` are optional. `skills` defaults to `[]`, for a brief that names no skill, and `thinkingLevel` to `null`, the model's default level. A `"pi"` worker adds `brief: "brief.md"`, and a watch adds `watch: { argv, cwd }` with an absolute `cwd` and an absolute path for any script in `argv`. `references/worker-assignment.md` holds one complete example per workspace mode and kind, so start from the closest one. The assignment's `role` picks the role instruction: `poteto`, `explorer`, `investigator`, `candidate`, `judge`, `verifier`, `reviewer`, `owner`, `watcher`, `comment-sicko`, or `general`. Its `workspace` is `{ mode: "worktree", inputCommit }` for a writable worker or `{ mode: "readonly", path }`, with an absolute `path`, for a worker limited to `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls`, `bash_readonly`, and MCP tools. `bash_readonly` is an OS-sandboxed read-only shell that allows `git`, `gh`, and network reads and blocks writes. Its `model` is a model spec or `inherit-parent`. Its `capabilities` default to `{ mcp: "inherit", env: "inherit", externalWrite: false }`, with `spawn` false. A container worker's `env` defaults to `"minimal"` instead: it holds its model provider's credential and the `PSTACK_` variables, and no other variable of yours. Name `env: "inherit"` to give it yours. A container worker that must clone a private repository, push, or run `gh` against the forge sets `capabilities.forge: true` as well (with `mcp`, `env`, and `externalWrite` named), which gives it your `gh` token and no other credential of yours. Spawn fails with `ForgeUnavailable` when you have no token to give. A default written as a family and level, such as `claude-opus-5-5-xhigh` or `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`, means that family's model at that thinking level, fast variant included. Spawn returns at once with a tmux attach command. A `pstack-worker` wake message reports each worker that settles. Then call `collect` for its report. Use `inspect` for live state, `steer` to redirect a live worker, and `abort` to stop one. A worker has no `pstack_worker` tool by default, so it does delegated work itself. A worker you assign `capabilities.spawn: true` has `pstack_worker` within the depth limit of three levels (you, it, and its workers). It owns its children's runs and receives their wakes, and its own children cannot get `capabilities.spawn: true`. A container worker has `workspace: { mode: "container", inputCommit }` and runs a writable clone of the pushed remote inside the container that `.pi/environment.json` configures, so `inputCommit` must be pushed first. Spawn refuses it with `ContainerUnavailable` when no container engine answers. Then a step that names a local fallback uses it, and a step without one reports itself blocked. A watch loop is a `pstack_worker` spawn with `kind: "watch"`. Its `watch.argv` runs in tmux in its `watch.cwd`, and its exit wakes you. A fixed interval uses `["sleep", "<seconds>"]`, and an event uses the watcher's command. A watch fires once. Spawn it again after each wake until the stop predicate holds. After a parent restart, re-arm each open watch loop from the run's `TODO.md` or plan, because nothing spawns it again on its own. The model rule is `~/.pi/agent/pstack/models.json`, and each of its role keys is a line.

spans.replacement:
# Pi session storage, resolved the way Pi resolves it (docs/sessions.md, docs/environment-variables.md), once per
# directory a session could have started in. Pi reads project settings from the session's working directory, so a
# worktree's own .pi/settings.json decides where its sessions live. For each directory:
# PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR, else the sessionDir setting with the project's .pi/settings.json over the agent
# directory's settings.json (an empty string in the project file still overrides the global one and means the
# default), else <agent directory>/sessions. A leading ~ is the home directory, file:// is a URL, and a relative
# sessionDir resolves from that directory.
pi_home() {
	case "$1" in
	"~") printf '%s\n' "$HOME" ;;
	"~"/*) printf '%s\n' "$HOME/${1#"~/"}" ;;
	file://*) printf '%b\n' "$(printf '%s' "${1#file://}" | sed 's/%\(..\)/\\x\1/g')" ;;
	*) printf '%s\n' "$1" ;;
	esac
}
agent_dir=$(pi_home "${PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR:-$HOME/.pi/agent}")
pi_session_dir() {
	local cwd=$1 dir="" settings value
	if [ -n "${PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR:-}" ]; then
		dir=$(pi_home "$PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR")
	else
		for settings in "$cwd/.pi/settings.json" "$agent_dir/settings.json"; do
			[ -f "$settings" ] || continue
			value=$(jq -r 'if (.sessionDir | type) == "string" then "s" + .sessionDir else "" end' "$settings" 2>/dev/null)
			if [ -n "$value" ]; then dir=$(pi_home "${value#s}"); break; fi
		done
		[ -z "$dir" ] && dir="$agent_dir/sessions"
	fi
	case "$dir" in /*) printf '%s\n' "$dir" ;; *) printf '%s\n' "$cwd/$dir" ;; esac
}
transcript_roots=()
while IFS= read -r start_dir; do
	[ -n "$start_dir" ] || continue
	root=$(pi_session_dir "$start_dir")
	[ -d "$root" ] || continue
	case " ${transcript_roots[*]-} " in *" $root "*) ;; *) transcript_roots+=("$root") ;; esac
done < <(printf '%s\n' "$invoked_from"; git worktree list --porcelain | awk '/^worktree /{print $2}')
